title: I’m a tech expert and new mum. Here’s what I learned testing 17 baby monitors
html:
Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need.

There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. Many are also wifi-enabled, meaning you can connect the monitor to your smartphone and view the live feed through an app instead of using a dedicated parent unit (read on for security advice).

With so many types of baby monitors to choose from, it can be tricky to distinguish the useful features from those that are simply nice to have. To cut through the noise, I tested 17 different models to help you find the best baby monitor for your needs.

At a glance

  • Best baby monitor overall
    Momcozy BM04 smart baby monitor

    £142.49 at John Lewis

  • Best budget baby monitor
    VTech VM6361HD video baby monitor

    £79.99 at John Lewis

  • Best over-the-cot baby monitor
    LeapFrog LF5817HD smart baby monitor

    £229.98 at John Lewis

  • Best baby health monitor
    Owlet Dream Sock smart baby monitor

    £198.99 at Amazon

Why you should trust me

I’ve been a technology journalist for 15 years, getting hands on with all kinds of consumer gadgets in that time. When I was expecting my first child, I flexed my product-testing muscles by reviewing pregnancy pillows and, after my baby was born, baby carriers. Testing baby monitors brings those two worlds together, combining my tech expertise with my experience as a new mum. To make sure my testing was informed by experts, I spoke with Jenny Ward, chief executive of the Lullaby Trust, for advice on safe sleep, and Alexis Hancock, director of engineering at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, about privacy and security.

How I tested

I temporarily turned my baby’s room into a panopticon of infant surveillance to put 17 baby monitors through their paces. Models were selected to cover a range of prices and features, with most of them including video.

I started by using a stopwatch app to time how long it took to get each monitor up and running. To test image quality, I set up each camera with a view into my child’s cot, using teddy bears as a stand-in for a live baby. I compared video streams for image clarity, consistency and colour, and I used blackout curtains to test night vision. I also placed a wireless speaker among the teddy bears and played a podcast to test sound quality.

While wifi-connected baby monitors should be viewable from anywhere you can connect to the internet, non-wifi models have a limited range. To test this, I took each non-wifi parent unit on a slow walk down my street and noted how far I got before connection was lost. To test the battery life of each parent unit – as well as one baby unit that could be used unplugged – I charged each device fully overnight before testing. I then set the screen to remain on continuously, rather than switching to sleep mode, and checked the parent units at hourly intervals, noting how long each took to run out of power.

Finally, I tested each baby monitor in real-world conditions, using it to keep an eye on my baby during naps and overnight sleeps.

The best baby monitors in 2026

Best baby monitor overall:
Momcozy BM04 smart baby monitor

A top performer for image and sound quality

The connected app isn’t the best

If you’re looking for a baby monitor that excels at the basics, offers wifi and non-wifi connections and doesn’t break the bank, this Momcozy monitor is an excellent choice. It’s a great all-rounder, coming top of the pack in my side-by-side tests for image and sound quality.

Why we love it
I set up this Momcozy monitor with a non-wifi connection in under four minutes: open the box, plug in the camera, and it pairs automatically with the parent unit. The video appeared crisp, with great colour contrast, and the sound was particularly clear; when I tested it overnight with my baby, it even picked up her hiccups. I was impressed by the wide range of the camera’s panning function, and it also has tilt and zoom functions. The parent unit provides decent battery life – about 10 hours with the screen constantly on – and a range that was more than sufficient to cover my house and garden.

This monitor is dual-mode, so you can connect it to wifi and view the feed through the Momcozy app or via the parent device. The app wasn’t the smoothest to use – the touchscreen buttons to pan and tilt felt clunky – but the image was clear.

It’s a shame that … the app somewhat lets down the smart functionality of the baby monitor. It seems designed for users who also have other Momcozy products, such as breast pumps, while the sign-up process prompted me to provide more personal info than I’m comfortable sharing, such as the baby’s birth date and milestones.

Wifi/non-wifi: both
Screen size: 5in
Video resolution: 1080p

A top performer for image and sound quality

The connected app isn’t the best

Best budget baby monitor:
VTech VM6361HD video baby monitor

Gets the basics right at a wallet-friendly price

Doesn’t have the greatest range

Tech company VTech offers a mind-boggling range of baby monitors. There are even more budget-friendly models than this one, but I found they compromised too much on quality. In my tests, this non-wifi baby monitor bested some more expensive options – and it’s still less than £100.

Why we love it
If you want the added security of a non-wifi baby monitor, which is less susceptible to remote hacking, or simply aren’t bothered about smart features, this VTech baby monitor is a good bet. Setup was a breeze, and the image quality was excellent, particularly in the dark. Despite being a less expensive model, it comes with a 5.5in screen. The camera features pan, tilt and zoom functions – useful for following a wriggly baby from one side of the cot to the other. Impressively, the battery on the parent unit lasted more than 12 hours, easily handling an overnight sleep unplugged.

It’s a shame that … this monitor didn’t have the greatest range in testing, losing its connection a couple of houses down the street, although it still adequately covered my entire house.

Wifi/non-wifi: non-wifi
Screen size: 5.5in
Video resolution: 720p

Gets the basics right at a wallet-friendly price

Doesn’t have the greatest range

Best over-the-cot baby monitor:
LeapFrog LF5817HD smart baby monitor

Large screen gives a clear view of baby at all times

Floor stand feels flimsy

While many baby units perch on a shelf, over-the-cot baby monitors are designed to be suspended over the baby’s cot for a bird’s-eye view. Set them up correctly, and you should be able to see the whole cot – ideal for a baby who moves a lot in the night. This LeapFrog model offers wifi and non-wifi options.

Why we love it
You can choose to use the LeapFrog over-the-cot monitor with its accompanying app, or keep it offline and view the video feed on the dedicated parent unit. I was immediately drawn to the latter, owing to its huge screen – a 7in display that felt like a small iPad in my hands. This size meant it was easy to get a clear view of the whole cot, with the image displaying good colour contrast, especially in night-vision mode.

The sound was slightly tinny in my podcast test, but there was no doubting its sensitivity: when I tried this monitor with my baby, it picked up seagulls cawing through the window. The parent unit also scored highest for range, and it had a battery life of more than 12 hours.

It’s a shame that … the floor stand, which holds the camera aloft, felt flimsier than the stands of other over-the-cot baby monitors I tested. To weight the base, you need to fill it with water – which is a faff.

Wifi/non-wifi: both
Screen size: 7in
Video resolution: 720p via parent screen, 1080p via app

Large screen gives a clear view of baby at all times

Floor stand feels flimsy

Best baby health monitor:
Owlet Dream Sock smart baby monitor

Smart sleep tracking helps with nap schedules

Fiddly to set up

First up: unless medically advised, you don’t need to monitor your baby’s breathing, heart rate or other health indicators, and there’s no evidence that doing so reduces the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (Sids). Some people find it reassuring to track such things; others may find it increases anxiety (see more below).

Nevertheless, these kinds of devices are having a moment: I tested baby monitors that track health metrics via wearables or mattress sensors, and the Owlet Dream Sock was my favourite. It wraps around baby’s foot with a Velcro-like fastening and includes a sensor that measures pulse rate, oxygen saturation and movement.

Why we love it
The Owlet has the air of a luxury tech product, with each item in the box nestled in premium packaging. The monitor is wifi-connected, so you’ll first need to download the app to set it up. The sock connects to a base station that sounds and flashes different alerts to indicate that the sock has lost connection or needs charging, or to show that your child is moving around a lot. The red alert sounds if your baby’s pulse rate or oxygen level falls outside a preset range.

The sock was easy to put on a wriggling baby and stayed put overnight. Luckily, I never heard the red alert while testing with my baby, and while the heart-rate and oxygen monitoring appeared to work fine, I didn’t have much use for this data. Where I found the Owlet monitor excelled was in its sleep tracking. The Owlet app noted when it thought my baby was awake, or in a light or deep sleep, and suggested nap times. I could imagine finding this useful for calculating wake windows when my baby was younger. For more insights, the sock can be paired with the Owlet Dream Sight camera baby monitor (sold together as the Owlet Dream Duo).

It’s a shame that … getting the sock connected took some troubleshooting, so this isn’t something to start setting up when bedtime is looming. You also need to keep the base station quite close to the sock to avoid the connection dropping.

Wifi/non-wifi: wifi
Screen size: not applicable
Video resolution: not applicable

Smart sleep tracking helps with nap schedules

Fiddly to set up

The best of the rest

Hubble Go Baby Portable smart video baby monitor

Flexible and rechargeable for on-the-go use

Parent unit is bulky for packing

Best for: travel

The Hubble Go Baby Portable was the only model I tested that had an unplugged option for the baby unit. It comes with a rechargeable battery pack that you can plug in to the camera, making it more easily portable. The flexible mount also twists into a stand or grip, so you can perch it in different spots while on the go. This smart version comes with wifi and non-wifi options; I particularly appreciated the physical switch on the camera to turn the wifi connection on and off.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the 5in parent unit is hefty for a travel option, weighing 250g (although you could just use the wifi mode for lighter packing). The camera battery, while useful, drains fairly quickly – within about eight hours in my tests, which meant it didn’t last a full night’s sleep.

Wifi/non-wifi: both; screen size: 5in; video resolution: 2K camera, 720p parent unit

Flexible and rechargeable for on-the-go use

Parent unit is bulky for packing

Nanit Pro camera baby monitor

App designed for tracking lots of data

Subscriptions are expensive on top of the base price

Best for: smart tracking

The Nanit baby monitor will appeal mainly to the data nerds out there who like to track as much as possible. An over-the-cot baby monitor, it uses computer vision and machine learning to generate sleep insights for individual sleeps and over the longer term. I found the app intuitive, despite the large amount of data on show.

The Nanit Pro comes with a “breathing band”, which you place around a young baby’s (0-3 months) chest. It features a geometric pattern that the overhead camera can use to detect breathing motion. For older babies, you can buy a sleeping bag separately with the same function.

It didn’t make the final cut because … Nanit’s subscription model didn’t sit well with me. The hardware isn’t cheap, and you’ll need a paid plan to access the full range of features; it starts with three months free, and then charges £10 a month. You can cancel the subscription and continue using the camera, but core features are limited mainly to real-time information.

Wifi/non-wifi: wifi; screen size: not applicable; video resolution: 1080p

App designed for tracking lots of data

Subscriptions are expensive on top of the base price

Momcozy BM03 video baby monitor

A high-performing, no-frills non-wifi baby monitor

The dual-mode Momcozy offers wifi at a similar price

Best for: non-wifi baby monitoring

It would be remiss not to mention this Momcozy baby monitor, given it was among the top performers in my tests for picture and sound quality. It was very easy to set up, taking less than five minutes to get the video feed up and running. The parent unit had a decent battery life and range, allowing me to walk several houses down my street before it lost connection.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the dual-mode Momcozy BM04 baby monitor is very similar, but comes with the additional option to connect to wifi if you wish. That said, if you expressly don’t want a wifi baby monitor, this is a solid choice.

Wifi/non-wifi: non-wifi; screen size: 5.5in; video resolution: 1080p
